During the nationally televised parade on January 20, Coleman was seen nodding toward the new president as the band marched past, followed a few steps later by a brief wave. "We had gone over and over time and again with everyone in the band that this was a military parade," Engle told the newspaper. "Protocol and proper decorum had to be followed at all times. Unfortunately, John chose to ignore that."

In a written statement, band manager Ken Rybka expressed dismay over the turn of events, describing Coleman’s sudden resignation as "a shock and surprise." Since the story broke, the band has been inundated with an influx of overwhelmingly critical phone calls, emails, and online comments—including public reactions on CNN’s iReport calling Coleman's gesture "a pretty cool thing."

"It is unfortunate that an internal band issue has raised so much discussion and ire from the general public," Rybka stated. "It has disheartened me more than you can imagine."

**WASHINGTON** — A pipe band drum major who led his unit down Pennsylvania Avenue during President Barack Obama’s historic 2009 inaugural parade has been suspended from performance duties after breaking strict parade protocol to acknowledge the new commander-in-chief.

Drum Major Colin Campbell, leading a high-profile highland pipe and drum band during the Jan. 20 festivities, received notice of his temporary suspension following an internal review by parade marshals and band leadership. 

The disciplinary action stems from a momentary breach of dress-and-effort etiquette as the band marched past the bulletproof glass reviewing stand outside the White House. 

According to parade guidelines, drum majors leading bands past the presidential box are required to execute a formal, rigid "Eyes Right" command. Protocol dictates that leaders hold their heads at a sharp 45-degree angle while maintaining a neutral, motionless facial expression—saluting with their mace without breaking form or offering personal greetings.

Instead, video coverage of the parade captured the moment Campbell caught President Obama’s eye. As the newly sworn-in president stood to applaud the pipers, Campbell offered a slight smile and a distinct, approving nod of the head before returning to form. While spectators along the route cheered the human moment on a freezing afternoon, military liaisons and band directors took a far stricter view.

"While we fully appreciate the emotion and historic magnitude of the day, individual departures from drill protocol undermine the collective presentation of the unit."

The suspension has ignited a fierce debate within the ceremonial marching community. Supporters of Campbell argue that the punishment is overly harsh for what amounted to a split-second courtesy during one of the most significant inaugurations in American history.

To suspend him over a head tilt seems completely devoid of perspective."

However, purists maintain that protocol exists precisely to prevent personal expressions from overshadowing the unit. 

"In a formal parade, you are not an individual; you represent the band and centuries of tradition," said an instructor with the Eastern United States Pipe Band Association, speaking on condition of anonymity. "If every drum major decides to wave, nod, or wink at the reviewing stand, the integrity of the parade dissolves."

Campbell, a 15-year veteran of the pipe band circuit who has performed at international tattoos and state occasions, declined to comment directly on the suspension, citing ongoing administrative review. However, colleagues close to the drum major say he has no regrets about the gesture.
